PERF-001.summary: Before optimizing, locate the hotspot with a benchmark or profile; do not change code on intuition.
PERF-001.details: Before changing performance-related code, use `go test -bench`, `go tool pprof`, or `runtime/pprof` to get data and confirm which section the hotspot falls in. A rewrite without data to support it does not enter the code: it may land on a path that is rarely taken, or sacrifice the readability of the common path for a rare case.
PERF-001.rationale: Performance problems only surface at runtime; reading code cannot tell which section is actually executed most. Optimizing on intuition often lands on the path you assume is slow but that is in fact rarely taken, so the change accomplishes nothing and leaves behind code that sacrificed readability for optimization. A benchmark and a profile give each function's share of time and allocations, concentrating the limited changes on the real hotspot.
PERF-001.detect_note: Check whether a performance change is accompanied by benchmark results or profile conclusions.

PERF-002.summary: Use strconv, not fmt, to convert between primitive types and strings.
PERF-002.details: Convert between int, uint, float, bool, and strings with `strconv` functions such as `Itoa`, `Atoi`, `FormatInt`, `ParseFloat`, and `FormatBool`. Use `fmt.Sprintf` only when multiple values and a complex format (such as a `%v` combination, width, and precision) are genuinely needed.
PERF-002.rationale: `fmt`'s formatting goes through interfaces and reflection on a general parsing path, allocating more and checking more than `strconv`'s dedicated functions. In Uber's benchmark the same conversion costs 143 ns/op and two allocations with `fmt.Sprint`, against 64.2 ns/op and one allocation with `strconv.Itoa`; on a high-frequency path the gap is amplified as it accumulates with the call count.
PERF-002.detect_note: Check whether conversions between a single primitive type and a string use fmt.

PERF-003.summary: Convert a fixed string to []byte once outside the loop and reuse the result.
PERF-003.details: When a loop or hot path repeatedly converts the same string literal or variable to `[]byte`, hoist the conversion out of the loop and reuse the result of that single conversion. When the string's content changes each iteration, or a slice that can be modified independently is needed, keep converting inside the loop.
PERF-003.rationale: Converting between string and `[]byte` allocates new memory and copies byte by byte. A fixed string converted inside a loop produces a slice that is discarded immediately each iteration, with allocations on the order of the loop count and the same amount of garbage added for the GC. In Uber's benchmark one conversion per iteration costs 22.2 ns/op, dropping to 3.25 ns/op once hoisted out of the loop.
PERF-003.detect_note: Check whether the loop contains conversions between string and []byte for a fixed string.

PERF-004.summary: When the number of elements is known or can be estimated, specify the slice capacity with make.
PERF-004.details: Use `make([]T, 0, n)` to initialize a slice that will be appended to, with n set to the known length or a reasonable upper bound. It is not required when the count cannot be estimated at all, or the slice is usually very small or short-lived.
PERF-004.rationale: Without a specified capacity, append starts from capacity 1 and grows step by step, allocating a new backing array and copying the old elements each round, with the old array turning into garbage right after. Once the capacity is accurate, only one allocation remains and both growth and copying are removed; when the capacity is a constant, from Go 1.26 this allocation can also land on the stack, doing away with the heap allocation and its corresponding GC burden as well.
PERF-004.detect_note: Check whether the make call for the slice an append targets carries a capacity argument.

PERF-005.summary: When the number of elements is known or can be estimated, pass a capacity hint to make(map).
PERF-005.details: Use `make(map[K]V, n)`, with n set to the known element count or a reasonable upper bound. It is not required when the count is unknown, or the map usually holds only a few elements. When the element set is fixed, write it out in one map literal rather than calling make first and assigning entry by entry.
PERF-005.rationale: Growing a map means re-bucketing and moving the existing keys and values into new buckets, so one growth allocates and moves more than a slice does. A capacity hint brings the initial bucket count close to the actual size and reduces the number of growths. The Uber text also states that it is only an approximation and does not guarantee a single allocation, so there is no need to force a value when the size clearly cannot be estimated.
PERF-005.detect_note: Check whether a map written entry by entry carries a capacity hint.

PERF-006.summary: Use strings.Builder to concatenate strings in a loop or across many operations, and call Grow first when the capacity can be estimated.
PERF-006.details: Use `strings.Builder` when building a string piece by piece (inside a loop, across many branches, with an indefinite count), and call `Grow` first when the result length can be estimated. Keep using `+` for a small, fixed inline concatenation. Use `bytes.Buffer` when a read-write buffer or `Bytes` access is needed.
PERF-006.rationale: Strings are immutable, so every += builds a new string and copies the whole accumulated content; inside a loop the repeated moving grows with the accumulated length, making the total copied close to quadratic. `Builder` writes into one mutable buffer and produces the result only once at retrieval; calling `Grow` before writing removes even the buffer growth.
PERF-006.detect_note: Check whether the loop contains string concatenation with +=.

PERF-007.summary: When keeping a small section of a large slice for a long time, use slices.Clone to cut the reference to the backing array.
PERF-007.details: `s[i:j]` shares the backing array with the original slice, so while the sub-slice is still referenced the whole array cannot be reclaimed. When the sub-slice lives long, or the original slice is far larger than the section needed, use `slices.Clone` (since Go 1.21) or `make` plus `copy` to produce an independent slice. When the sub-slice is released as the function returns, or covers most of the elements anyway, slicing directly is enough.
PERF-007.rationale: When a small section is cut out of a large file or large response and kept for a long time, the sub-slice still points at the original backing array, the GC treats the whole array as still referenced, and the process's resident memory far exceeds what is actually needed. `Clone` copies out an independent array containing only the needed elements, and the original array can be reclaimed once it loses its references.
PERF-007.detect_note: Check whether a sub-slice cut from a large buffer and kept for a long time is copied.

PERF-008.summary: Pass arguments by value when the function only reads them through a dereference; do not pass pointers just to save a few bytes.
PERF-008.details: A string, an interface value, and a small struct are themselves only a machine word in size, so passing by value and passing a pointer cost about the same to copy. Pass by value when the function body only reads through `*p` and never writes. Pass a pointer when the caller's data must be modified, or the struct is clearly large.
PERF-008.rationale: A string and an interface value are fixed-size headers whose copy cost equals that of passing a pointer, with one less dereference. Passing `*string` or `*io.Reader` to save bytes adds a layer of indirection, and when the pointer escapes the function it can push the data onto the heap, actually increasing allocations.
PERF-008.detect_note: Check whether a parameter that is only read through a dereference uses a pointer.

PERF-009.summary: Production code does not compare with reflect.DeepEqual.
PERF-009.details:
Type-known comparisons use the typed Equal functions.

- `slices.Equal` for slices, `maps.Equal` for maps, `bytes.Equal` for byte strings
- `reflect.DeepEqual` walks reflection and runs 50–200x slower
- Test code comparing expected values is exempt (semantics first)
PERF-009.rationale: DeepEqual reflects over the value structure at runtime, costing one to two orders of magnitude more than typed comparison on hot paths; the typed Equal functions in the slices and maps packages are compiler-specialized, with the same semantics at near hand-written-loop cost.
PERF-009.detect_note: Check DeepEqual calls on production paths

PERF-010.summary: regexp and template compile once at package level.
PERF-010.details:
Compiled artifacts are reused, not rebuilt in function bodies.

- Package-level `var re = regexp.MustCompile(...)`, with functions only referencing it
- Repeated Compile inside functions costs roughly an order of magnitude more and always allocates
- template's `Parse` follows the same rule
PERF-010.rationale: Compile parses the regex and builds the state machine on every call, an overhead comparable to the matching itself on hot paths; the official documentation writes the package-level initialization case into MustCompile's description — compile once and reuse is its designed use.
PERF-010.detect_note: Check for regexp.Compile and template.Parse inside function bodies

PERF-011.summary: Unbounded inputs are processed streaming, not loaded whole with io.ReadAll.
PERF-011.details:
Memory peaks follow the input's upper bound, not its current size.

- Large files and unbounded responses stream with `bufio.Scanner` and `io.Copy`
- `io.ReadAll` is for bounded, small inputs only (such as a small config)
- Unbounded means the maximum size cannot be known before the call
PERF-011.rationale: ReadAll piles the whole input into memory, and with unbounded inputs (external URLs, user uploads) the memory peak is handed to the peer or an attacker; streaming keeps memory usage constant, decoupled from input scale.
PERF-011.detect_note: Check whether io.ReadAll inputs are bounded

PERF-012.summary: A reused http.Client sets Timeout explicitly and customizes its Transport.
PERF-012.details:
Client and Transport are process-level configuration points.

- A zero-value Client has no timeout; requests may hang forever
- The default Transport's `MaxIdleConnsPerHost` is only 2, so high concurrency queues for connections
- A package-level singleton Client is configured centrally, never created ad hoc at call sites
PERF-012.rationale: The connection pool is the Client's internal state: creating a Client per call rebuilds the pool and discards every reusable keep-alive connection, and a zero-value Client with no timeout turns an unresponsive downstream into a goroutine leak.
PERF-012.detect_note: Check the configuration of package-level http.Clients

PERF-013.summary: Handle resp.Body by version: Go 1.27+ reclaims on Close; earlier versions must drain it.
PERF-013.details:
Connection reuse depends on the body's read state.

- Go 1.27+ automatically drains unread content on Body close (within a conservative limit); manual draining is unnecessary
- To abandon a very large body, or on Go 1.26 and below, `io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)` before `Close`
- Every response must be `Close`d whether or not its content is read
PERF-013.rationale: A keep-alive connection returns to the pool only after its body is drained, and undrained connections are torn down and rebuilt; since Go 1.27, Close drains automatically, fixing the performance trap — but bodies beyond the automatic limit still need explicit handling.
PERF-013.detect_note: Check body handling in HTTP client code

PERF-014.summary: Range over maps taking the value variable, not a second subscript lookup.
PERF-014.details:
for k, v := range m hashes once per iteration.

- When the value is needed, use the loop variable v, not `m[k]`
- When only keys are needed, use `for k := range m`
- `m[k]` inside the loop body re-hashes every iteration
PERF-014.rationale: The second range variable is the element already fetched during iteration, while m[k] re-hashes the key every round; in hot loops it is pure waste, and the form carries no compensating benefit.

PERF-016.summary: sql.DB connection pool limits and lifetimes are configured explicitly.
PERF-016.details:
Pool parameters default to no protection.

- Set `MaxOpenConns`, `MaxIdleConns`, `ConnMaxLifetime`, and `ConnMaxIdleTime` explicitly
- Defaults are unlimited connections that never expire, so a failure piles connections up and crushes the database
- Values follow the database connection limit and instance replica count, with notes
PERF-016.rationale: An unlimited default means every goroutine can hold a connection, so amplified failures crush the database before the application; explicit limits keep failure behavior bounded, and ConnMaxLifetime rotates connections to avoid database-side aging.
